prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Academy Award-winning composer Maurice Jarre, who scored movies including "Doctor Zhivago" and "Lawrence of Arabia" among others, died Sunday from cancer in Los Angeles. He was 84. Movie composer Maurice Jarre pictured at the Berlin International Film Festival last month. Jarre enjoyed an illustrious career, working with Hollywood directing legends including John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock and, most notably, David Lean. Fellow French composer Alexandre Desplat, who interviewed Jarre for The Screening Room at the Berlin International Film Festival last month, told CNN Monday: "Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of the melody and a benevolent human being."  Watch tribute to Maurice Jarre » . Jarre won Oscars in 1963 and 1966 for his collaborations on the Lean movies "Lawrence of Arabia" and "Doctor Zhivago" respectively. He then mustered a further six Oscar nominations but his third award came once again through a further collaboration with Lean on " A Passage to India" in 1984. He then swapped orchestral composition to become a pioneer of electronic scoring, working on the music for, among others, "Ghost," "Witness," "Dead Poet's Society" and "Fatal Attraction." At the same time his son Jean-Michel Jarre became one of the world's best known electronic musicians with global hits such as "Oxygene" and huge outdoor concerts. His final movie composition was for the 2000 film "I Dreamed of Africa." Jarre's career included symphonies, ballet and theatre but it was for his 150 film scores that he was presented with an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month - almost half a century after producer Sam Spiegel hired him to work on "Lawrence of Arabia." Festival director Dieter Kosslick said in a statement late last year: "Film composers often are in the shadows of great directors and acting stars. It's different with Maurice Jarre; the music of 'Doctor Zhivago,' like much of his work, is world-famous and remains unforgotten in the history of cinema." Speaking in Berlin to double-Oscar nominee Desplat -- who himself scored "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" and "The Queen" -- Jarre said: "I never really had a 'bust-up' with a good director. A good director will always find an intellectual understanding. And that's what was great - I had an opportunity with all these people. I don't think I can say that I ever worked with a bad director." But Jarre also said that directing legends of the rank of Huston and Hitchock had disappeared and no longer existed, adding: "The only problem is now, there is more and more bad music that goes 'dang dang dang dang dang...' So...it's better to turn off the music, and listen to a concert of Mozart." Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Academy Award-winning composer Maurice Jarre, who scored films including “Doctor Zhivago” and “Lawrence of Arabia,” died of cancer Sunday in Los Angeles. He was 84.

Movie composer Maurice Jarre was pictured at the Berlin International Film Festival last month.

Jarre enjoyed an illustrious career, working with legendary Hollywood directors including John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock and, most notably, David Lean.

Fellow French composer Alexandre Desplat, who interviewed Jarre for *The Screening Room* at the Berlin International Film Festival last month, told CNN on Monday: “Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of the melody and a benevolent human being.”

Watch a tribute to Maurice Jarre »

Jarre won Oscars in 1963 and 1966 for his work on Lean’s “Lawrence of Arabia” and “Doctor Zhivago,” respectively. He went on to earn six more Oscar nominations, but his third win came through another collaboration with Lean, on “A Passage to India” in 1984.

He later moved away from orchestral composition to become a pioneer of electronic scoring, creating music for films including “Ghost,” “Witness,” “Dead Poets Society” and “Fatal Attraction.”

At the same time, his son Jean-Michel Jarre became one of the world’s best-known electronic musicians, achieving global success with works such as “Oxygène” and staging huge outdoor concerts.

Jarre’s final film score was for the 2000 movie “I Dreamed of Africa.”

His career also encompassed symphonies, ballet and theater, but it was in recognition of his 150 film scores that he received an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month—almost half a century after producer Sam Spiegel hired him to work on “Lawrence of Arabia.”

Festival director Dieter Kosslick said in a statement late last year: “Film composers often are in the shadows of great directors and acting stars. It’s different with Maurice Jarre; the music of ‘Doctor Zhivago,’ like much of his work, is world-famous and remains unforgotten in the history of cinema.”

Speaking in Berlin with two-time Oscar nominee Desplat—who himself scored “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button” and “The Queen”—Jarre said: “I never really had a ‘bust-up’ with a good director. A good director will always find an intellectual understanding. And that’s what was great—I had an opportunity with all these people. I don’t think I can say that I ever worked with a bad director.”

But Jarre also said that directors of the caliber of Huston and Hitchcock had disappeared and no longer existed, adding: “The only problem is now, there is more and more bad music that goes ‘dang dang dang dang dang...’ So... it’s better to turn off the music, and listen to a concert of Mozart.”

Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Maurice Jarre, the Oscar-winning composer behind the music for films such as “Lawrence of Arabia” and “Doctor Zhivago,” died of cancer in Los Angeles on Sunday. He was 84.

Jarre, who was photographed at the Berlin International Film Festival the previous month, had a distinguished career that included collaborations with celebrated directors such as Alfred Hitchcock, John Huston and, above all, David Lean.

French composer Alexandre Desplat interviewed Jarre in Berlin for *The Screening Room* shortly before his death. On Monday, Desplat told CNN that Jarre was “an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of the melody and a benevolent human being.”

Jarre received Academy Awards in 1963 and 1966 for his work with Lean on “Lawrence of Arabia” and “Doctor Zhivago,” respectively. Six additional Oscar nominations followed. He earned his third Academy Award in 1984, again for a Lean film, “A Passage to India.”

Later, Jarre moved away from traditional orchestral writing and became an early innovator in electronic film scoring. His credits from that period included “Ghost,” “Witness,” “Dead Poets Society” and “Fatal Attraction.”

Meanwhile, his son, Jean-Michel Jarre, rose to international prominence as an electronic musician, known for worldwide hits including “Oxygene” and for staging enormous outdoor performances.

Maurice Jarre’s last film score was written for the 2000 movie “I Dreamed of Africa.” Although his body of work also encompassed symphonies, ballet and theater, he was best known for composing music for 150 films. That achievement was recognized with an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival the month before his death—nearly 50 years after producer Sam Spiegel selected him to score “Lawrence of Arabia.”

In a statement issued late the previous year, festival director Dieter Kosslick observed that film composers are frequently overshadowed by prominent directors and actors. He said Jarre was an exception, noting that the music from “Doctor Zhivago,” along with much of the composer’s other work, had become famous worldwide and held an enduring place in cinema history.

During his Berlin conversation with Desplat—a two-time Oscar nominee whose own credits included “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button” and “The Queen”—Jarre said he had never experienced a serious conflict with a talented director. In his view, a strong director would always be capable of reaching an intellectual understanding. He added that he had been fortunate to work with all of those filmmakers and did not believe he had ever collaborated with a bad director.

Jarre also lamented that directors of Huston’s and Hitchcock’s stature had vanished. He criticized the growing prevalence of poor film music that simply went “dang dang dang dang dang,” suggesting that it would be preferable to switch it off and listen to a Mozart concert instead.

Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to the report.

Born in Lyon in 1924, Jarre began his professional life in the theater before moving into film. He achieved international fame through his partnership with British director David Lean, composing the music for “Lawrence of Arabia,” “Doctor Zhivago,” “Ryan’s Daughter” and “A Passage to India.” His majestic orchestral score for “Lawrence of Arabia” captured the scale and mystery of the desert, while the romantic “Lara’s Theme” from “Doctor Zhivago” became a worldwide popular success.

Jarre won three Academy Awards, for “Lawrence of Arabia,” “Doctor Zhivago” and “A Passage to India.” Over the course of his career, he wrote roughly 150 film scores and worked with prominent filmmakers including Alfred Hitchcock, John Huston and Peter Weir. His music accompanied productions ranging from historical epics and dramas to thrillers and adventure films.

Although best known for expansive orchestral compositions, Jarre continually experimented with new sounds. In later years he embraced synthesizers and electronic instruments, creating innovative scores for films such as “Witness,” “The Mosquito Coast” and “Dead Poets Society.” That evolution demonstrated his ability to adapt his style while preserving the strong melodies and dramatic sensitivity that defined his work.

Shortly before his death, the Berlin International Film Festival honored Jarre with an honorary Golden Bear for lifetime achievement. Together with his three Oscars and extensive body of work, the award reflected the global reach of his music. **LOS ANGELES, March 30, 2009** — Maurice Jarre, the French composer whose sweeping scores for *Lawrence of Arabia* and *Doctor Zhivago* helped define the sound of epic cinema, has died of cancer. He was 84.

Jarre died Saturday in Los Angeles, according to his family. During a career spanning more than five decades, he composed music for more than 150 films and became one of Hollywood’s most celebrated composers.

He won three Academy Awards, all for films directed by David Lean: *Lawrence of Arabia* in 1962, *Doctor Zhivago* in 1965 and *A Passage to India* in 1984. Jarre received nine Oscar nominations overall.

His partnership with Lean was among the most important composer-director collaborations in film history. In addition to the three Oscar-winning scores, Jarre wrote the music for Lean’s *Ryan’s Daughter*. His grand orchestral themes complemented the director’s expansive landscapes and emotionally charged storytelling. The haunting “Lara’s Theme” from *Doctor Zhivago* became internationally famous and was later adapted into the popular song “Somewhere, My Love.”

Jarre’s other major credits included *The Longest Day*, *The Message*, *Witness*, *Fatal Attraction*, *Dead Poets Society* and *Ghost*. Although best known for lush symphonic writing, he also embraced electronic instruments and unconventional sounds, particularly in his later work.

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre studied percussion and composition at the Paris Conservatory before working in theater and film. His ability to combine memorable melodies, bold instrumentation and a strong sense of drama influenced generations of screen composers and demonstrated how music could become an essential part of a film’s identity.

Jarre was the father of electronic-music pioneer Jean-Michel Jarre. His legacy endures in some of cinema’s most recognizable and emotionally powerful scores.

**Maurice Jarre, Oscar-winning composer of ‘Lawrence of Arabia,’ dies at 84**

Maurice Jarre, the French composer whose sweeping scores for “Lawrence of Arabia” and “Doctor Zhivago” became as memorable as the films themselves, died March 28, 2009, in Los Angeles after a battle with cancer. He was 84.

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre began studying music relatively late, enrolling at the Paris Conservatory after initially pursuing engineering. He established his reputation in French theater before director David Lean brought him to international prominence with the score for 1962’s “Lawrence of Arabia.”

Jarre went on to win three Academy Awards, all for Lean films: “Lawrence of Arabia,” “Doctor Zhivago” and “A Passage to India.” “Lara’s Theme” from “Doctor Zhivago” became a worldwide standard, while his bold use of percussion and expansive orchestration helped define the sound of the modern historical epic.

His résumé included more than 150 film and television scores, among them “The Longest Day,” “The Man Who Would Be King,” “Witness,” “Fatal Attraction,” “Gorillas in the Mist” and “Dead Poets Society.” He also embraced electronic music later in his career, showing a versatility that kept his work relevant across several decades.

French composer Alexandre Desplat hailed Jarre as “one of the great masters of film music,” crediting him with helping open Hollywood’s doors to later generations of French composers.

Weeks before his death, Jarre made one of his final public appearances at the Berlin International Film Festival, where he received an honorary Golden Bear for lifetime achievement. The festival declared that “film music history is unthinkable without Maurice Jarre,” recognizing a career that gave some of cinema’s grandest images their emotional force.

Jarre was the father of electronic-music pioneer Jean-Michel Jarre. His legacy endures in melodies that reached far beyond the screen — music that could evoke deserts, revolutions, romance and loss in only a few notes.
